questions.q: In Problem 1, why is {[2, 1], [4, 2]} linearly dependent?
options: Because [4, 2] = 2*[2, 1], making the determinant (2)(2)-(1)(4) = 0
Because both vectors contain a 2
Because the vectors have different lengths
Because determinants only apply to independent sets
questions.explain: The determinant (2)(2)-(1)(4) = 4-4 = 0, and directly, [4,2] is exactly twice [2,1], so the pair lies on a single line and cannot span all of R^2.

questions.q: In Problem 2, normalizing [1, 1] produces which well-known quantum state?
options: The |+> state, [1/sqrt(2), 1/sqrt(2)], the equal superposition of |0> and |1>
The |0> state, [1, 0]
The |1> state, [0, 1]
No recognizable quantum state -- it's just an arbitrary normalized vector
questions.explain: [1,1] has norm sqrt(2), and dividing by sqrt(2) gives [1/sqrt(2), 1/sqrt(2)], which is exactly the |+> state used throughout quantum computing for an equal 50/50 superposition.

questions.q: In Problem 3, what coordinates (a, b) express [4, 2] in the basis {[1,1], [1,-1]}?
questions.explain: Solving a+b=4 and a-b=2 gives 2a=6 so a=3, then b=1; checking, 3*[1,1]+1*[1,-1] = [4,2], matching the target.

questions.q: In Problem 4, the 3x3 determinant of {[1,2,0],[0,1,3],[2,0,1]} works out to 13. What does this confirm?
options: The three vectors are linearly independent and form a valid basis for R^3
The three vectors are linearly dependent
The vectors all lie in the same plane
The calculation is invalid because determinants cannot be positive
questions.explain: A nonzero 3x3 determinant (13) for three vectors in R^3 confirms linear independence, meaning none of the three vectors can be written as a combination of the other two.

questions.q: Why does the lab point out that Problem 3's result, (3, 1), differs from Lesson 4's worked example result, (3, 2), even though both use the same basis {[1,1],[1,-1]}?
options: Because the two problems use different target vectors ([4,2] vs [5,1]), so the change-of-basis coordinates are specific to each target vector, not a fixed shortcut reusable across vectors
Because one of the two results must be a calculation error
Because the basis itself changed between the two problems
Because change-of-basis coordinates are always random
questions.explain: The same basis can produce different coordinate pairs for different target vectors -- [5,1] maps to (3,2) in Lesson 4 while the fresh target [4,2] maps to (3,1) here, since the underlying vector being expressed is different each time.
